entries.5c13e88027360b21bc0f9a95533031192982043e: <div sID="gen7733" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="11" osisID="1Chr.11" sID="1Chr.11"/> <div eID="gen7733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7734" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen7735" type="x-p"/> In this chapter is repeated, I. The elevation of David to the throne, immediately upon the death of Saul, by common consent, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.1-1Chr.11.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. His gaining the castle of Zion out of the hands of the Jebusites, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.4-1Chr.11.9">ver. 4-9</reference>. III. The catalogue of the worthies and great men of his kingdom, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.10-1Chr.11.47">ver. 10-47</reference>.
entries.fb9817e30b56e08470f4c19286a1e69ddbe37f66: <div eID="gen7735" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen7734" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">David's Accession to the Throne. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1055.)</title> <div sID="gen7736" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then all Israel gathered themselves to David unto Hebron, saying, Behold, we <hi type="italic">are</hi> thy bone and thy flesh. <hi type="super">2</hi> And moreover in time past, even when Saul was king, thou <hi type="italic">wast</hi> he that leddest out and broughtest in Israel: and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God said unto thee, Thou shalt feed my people Israel, and thou shalt be ruler over my people Israel. <hi type="super">3</hi> Therefore came all the elders of Israel to the king to Hebron; and David made a covenant with them in Hebron before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; and they anointed David king over Israel, according to the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> by Samuel. <hi type="super">4</hi> And David and all Israel went to Jerusalem, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> Jebus; where the Jebusites <hi type="italic">were,</hi> the inhabitants of the land. <hi type="super">5</hi> And the inhabitants of Jebus said to David, Thou shalt not come hither. Nevertheless David took the castle of Zion, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> the city of David. <hi type="super">6</hi> And David said, Whosoever smiteth the Jebusites first shall be chief and captain. So Joab the son of Zeruiah went first up, and was chief. <hi type="super">7</hi> And David dwelt in the castle; therefore they called it the city of David. <hi type="super">8</hi> And he built the city round about, even from Millo round about: and Joab repaired the rest of the city. <hi type="super">9</hi> So David waxed greater and greater: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts <hi type="italic">was</hi> with him. <div eID="gen7736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7737" type="x-p"/> David is here brought to the possession. <div eID="gen7737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7738" type="x-p"/> I. Of the throne of Israel, after he had reigned seven years in Hebron, over Judah only. In consideration of his relation to them (<reference osisRef="1Chr.11.1">v. 1</reference>), his former good services, and especially the divine designation (<reference osisRef="1Chr.11.2">v. 2</reference>), they anointed him their king: he covenanted to protect them, and they to bear faith and true allegiance to him, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.3">v. 3</reference>. Observe, 1. God's counsels will be fulfilled at last, whatever difficulties lie in the way. If God had said, <hi type="italic">David shall rule,</hi> it is in vain to oppose it. 2. Men that have long stood in their own light, when they have long wearied themselves with their lying vanities, it is to be hoped, will understand the things that belong to their peace and return to <hi type="italic">their own mercies.</hi> 3. Between prince and people there is an original contract, which both ought religiously to observe. If ever any prince might have claimed an absolute despotic power, David might, and might as safely as any have been entrusted with it; and yet he made a covenant with the people, took the coronation-oath, to rule by law. <div eID="gen7738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7739" type="x-p"/> II. Of the strong-hold of Zion, which was held by the Jebusites till David's time. Whether David had a particular eye upon it as a place fit to make a royal city, or whether he had a promise of it from God, it seems that one of his first exploits was to make himself master of that fort; and, when he had it, he called it the <hi type="italic">city of David,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.7">v. 7</reference>. To this reference is had, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">Ps. ii. 6</reference>. <hi type="italic">I have set my king upon my holy hill of Zion.</hi> See here what quickens and engages resolution in great undertakings. 1. Opposition. When the Jebusites set David at defiance, and said, <hi type="italic">Thou shalt not come hither.</hi> he resolved to force it, whatever it cost him. 2. Prospect of preferment. When David proposed to give the general's place to him that would lead the attack upon the castle of Zion, Joab was fired with the proposal, and he <hi type="italic">went up first, and was chief.</hi> It has been said, "Take away honour out of the soldier's eye and you cut off the spurs from his heels."
entries.0c585fefe50dded9042f89472416ba4a13ea3d3a: <div eID="gen7739" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">David's Mighty Men. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1048.)</title> <div sID="gen7740" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> These also <hi type="italic">are</hi> the chief of the mighty men whom David had, who strengthened themselves with him in his kingdom, <hi type="italic">and</hi> with all Israel, to make him king, according to the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> concerning Israel. <hi type="super">11</hi> And this <hi type="italic">is</hi> the number of the mighty men whom David had; Jashobeam, a Hachmonite, the chief of the captains: he lifted up his spear against three hundred slain <hi type="italic">by him</hi> at one time. <hi type="super">12</hi> And after him <hi type="italic">was</hi> Eleazar the son of Dodo, the Ahohite, who <hi type="italic">was one</hi> of the three mighties. <hi type="super">13</hi> He was with David at Pas-dammim, and there the Philistines were gathered together to battle, where was a parcel of ground full of barley; and the people fled from before the Philistines. <hi type="super">14</hi> And they set themselves in the midst of <hi type="italic">that</hi> parcel, and delivered it, and slew the Philistines; and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> saved <hi type="italic">them</hi> by a great deliverance. <hi type="super">15</hi> Now three of the thirty captains went down to the rock to David, into the cave of Adullam; and the host of the Philistines encamped in the valley of Rephaim. <hi type="super">16</hi> And David <hi type="italic">was</hi> then in the hold, and the Philistines' garrison <hi type="italic">was</hi> then at Bethlehem. <hi type="super">17</hi> And David longed, and said, Oh that one would give me drink of the water of the well of Bethlehem, that <hi type="italic">is</hi> at the gate! <hi type="super">18</hi> And the three brake through the host of the Philistines, and drew water out of the well of Bethlehem, that <hi type="italic">was</hi> by the gate, and took <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and brought <hi type="italic">it</hi> to David: but David would not drink <hi type="italic">of</hi> it, but poured it out to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="super">19</hi> And said, My God forbid it me, that I should do this thing: shall I drink the blood of these men that have put their lives in jeopardy? for with <hi type="italic">the jeopardy of</hi> their lives they brought it. Therefore he would not drink it. These things did these three mightiest. <hi type="super">20</hi> And Abishai the brother of Joab, he was chief of the three: for lifting up his spear against three hundred, he slew <hi type="italic">them,</hi> and had a name among the three. <hi type="super">21</hi> Of the three, he was more honourable than the two; for he was their captain: howbeit he attained not to the <hi type="italic">first</hi> three. <hi type="super">22</hi> Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, the son of a valiant man of Kabzeel, who had done many acts; he slew two lionlike men of Moab: also he went down and slew a lion in a pit in a snowy day. <hi type="super">23</hi> And he slew an Egyptian, a man of <hi type="italic">great</hi> stature, five cubits high; and in the Egyptian's hand <hi type="italic">was</hi> a spear like a weaver's beam; and he went down to him with a staff, and plucked the spear out of the Egyptian's hand, and slew him with his own spear. <hi type="super">24</hi> These <hi type="italic">things</hi> did Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and had the name among the three mighties. <hi type="super">25</hi> Behold, he was honourable among the thirty, but attained not to the <hi type="italic">first</hi> three: and David set him over his guard. <hi type="super">26</hi> Also the valiant men of the armies <hi type="italic">were,</hi> Asahel the brother of Joab, Elhanan the son of Dodo of Bethlehem, <hi type="super">27</hi> Shammoth the Harorite, Helez the Pelonite, <hi type="super">28</hi> Ira the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite, Abiezer the Antothite, <hi type="super">29</hi> Sibbecai the Hushathite, Ilai the Ahohite, <hi type="super">30</hi> Maharai the Netophathite, Heled the son of Baanah the Netophathite, <hi type="super">31</hi> Ithai the son of Ribai of Gibeah, <hi type="italic">that pertained</hi> to the children of Benjamin, Benaiah the Pirathonite, <hi type="super">32</hi> Hurai of the brooks of Gaash, Abiel the Arbathite, <hi type="super">33</hi> Azmaveth the Baharumite, Eliahba the Shaalbonite, <hi type="super">34</hi> The sons of Hashem the Gizonite, Jonathan the son of Shage the Hararite, <hi type="super">35</hi> Ahiam the son of Sacar the Hararite, Eliphal the son of Ur, <hi type="super">36</hi> Hepher the Mecherathite, Ahijah the Pelonite, <hi type="super">37</hi> Hezro the Carmelite, Naarai the son of Ezbai, <hi type="super">38</hi> Joel the brother of Nathan, Mibhar the son of Haggeri, <hi type="super">39</hi> Zelek the Ammonite, Naharai the Berothite, the armourbearer of Joab the son of Zeruiah, <hi type="super">40</hi> Ira the Ithrite, Gareb the Ithrite, <hi type="super">41</hi> Uriah the Hittite, Zabad the son of Ahlai, <hi type="super">42</hi> Adina the son of Shiza the Reubenite, a captain of the Reubenites, and thirty with him, <hi type="super">43</hi> Hanan the son of Maachah, and Joshaphat the Mithnite, <hi type="super">44</hi> Uzzia the Ashterathite, Shama and Jehiel the sons of Hothan the Aroerite, <hi type="super">45</hi> Jediael the son of Shimri, and Joha his brother, the Tizite, <hi type="super">46</hi> Eliel the Mahavite, and Jeribai, and Joshaviah, the sons of Elnaam, and Ithmah the Moabite, <hi type="super">47</hi> Eliel, and Obed, and Jasiel the Mesobaite. <div eID="gen7740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7741" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of David's worthies, the great men of his time that served him and were preferred by him. The first edition of this catalogue we had, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.8-2Sam.23.39">2 Sam. xxiii. 8</reference>, &c. This is much the same, only that those named here from <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.41-1Chr.11.47">v. 41</reference> to the end are added. Observe, <div eID="gen7741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7742" type="x-p"/> I. The connexion of this catalogue with that which is said concerning David, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.9">v. 9</reference>. 1. <hi type="italic">David waxed greater and greater,</hi> and these were his mighty men. Much of the strength and honour of great men is borrowed from their servants and depends upon them, which cannot but somewhat diminish pomp and power in the opinion of those that are wise. David is great because he has great men about him; take these away, and he is where he was. 2. <hi type="italic">The Lord of hosts was with him, and these were the mighty men which he had.</hi> God was with him and wrought for him, but by men and means and the use of second causes. By <hi type="italic">this</hi> it appeared that God was with him, that he inclined the hearts of those to come over to him that were able to serve his interest. As, if God be for us none can be against us, so, if God be for us, all shall be for us that we have occasion for. Yet David ascribed his success and increase, not to the hosts he had, but to the <hi type="italic">Lord of hosts,</hi> not to the mighty men that were with him, but to the mighty God whose presence with us is all in all. <div eID="gen7742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7743" type="x-p"/> II. The title of this catalogue (<reference osisRef="1Chr.11.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">These are the men who strengthened themselves with him.</hi> In strengthening him they strengthened themselves and their own interest; for his advancement was theirs. What we do in our places for the support of the kingdom of the Son of David we shall be gainers by. In strengthening it we strengthen ourselves. It may be read, <hi type="italic">They held strongly with him and with all Israel.</hi> Note, When God has work to do he will not want fit instruments to do it with. If it be work that requires mighty men, mighty men shall either be found or made to effect it, <hi type="italic">according to the word of the Lord.</hi> <div eID="gen7743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7744" type="x-p"/> III. That which made all these men honourable was the good service that they did to their king and country; they helped to make David king (<reference osisRef="1Chr.11.10">v. 10</reference>)—a good work. They slew the Philistines, and other public enemies, and were instrumental to save Israel. Note, The way to be great is to do good. Nor did they gain this honour without labour and the hazard of their lives. The honours of Christ's kingdom are prepared for those that <hi type="italic">fight the good fight of faith,</hi> that labour and suffer, and are willing to venture all, even life itself, for Christ and a good conscience. It is by a patient continuance in well-doing that we must seek for glory, and honour, and immortality; and those that are faithful to the Son of David shall find their names registered and enrolled much more to their honour than these are in the records of fame. <div eID="gen7744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7745" type="x-p"/> IV. Among all the great exploits of David's mighty men, here is nothing great mentioned concerning David himself but his <hi type="italic">pouring out water before the Lord</hi> which he had <hi type="italic">longed for,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.18-1Chr.11.19">v. 18, 19</reference>. Four very honourable dispositions of David appeared in that action, which, for aught I know, made it as great as any of the achievements of those worthies. 1. Repentance for his own weakness. It is really an honour to a man, when he is made sensible that he has said or done any thing unadvisedly, to unsay it and undo it again by repentance, as it is a shame to a man when he has said or done amiss to stand to it. 2. Denial of his own appetite. He longed for the water of the well of Bethlehem; but, when he had it, he would not drink it, because he would not so far humour himself and gratify a foolish fancy. He that has such a rule as this <hi type="italic">over his own spirit is better than the mighty.</hi> It is an honour to a man to have the command of himself; but he that will command himself must sometimes cross himself. 3. Devotion towards God. That water which he thought too good, too precious, for his own drinking, he <hi type="italic">poured out to the Lord</hi> for a <hi type="italic">drink offering.</hi> If we have any thing better than another, let God be honoured with it, who is the best, and should have the best. 4. Tenderness of his servants. It put him into the greatest confusion imaginable to think that three brave men should hazard their lives to fetch water for him. In his account it turns the water into blood. It is the honour of great men not to be prodigal of the blood of those they employ, but, in all the commands they give them, to put their own souls into their souls' stead. <div eID="gen7745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7746" type="x-p"/> V. In the wonderful achievements of these heroes the power of God must be acknowledged. How could one slay 300 and another the same number (<reference osisRef="1Chr.11.11">v. 11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.20">20</reference>), another two lion-like men (<reference osisRef="1Chr.11.22">v. 22</reference>), and another an Egyptian giant (<reference osisRef="1Chr.11.23">v. 23</reference>), if they had not had the extraordinary presence of God with them, according to that promise, <reference osisRef="Josh.23.10">Josh. xxiii. 10</reference>, <hi type="italic">One man of you shall chase a thousand, for the Lord your God fighteth for you?</hi> <div eID="gen7746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7747" type="x-p"/> VI. One of these worthies is said to be <hi type="italic">an Ammonite</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Chr.11.39">v. 39</reference>), another <hi type="italic">a Moabite</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Chr.11.46">v. 46</reference>), and yet the law was that an <hi type="italic">Ammonite</hi> and <hi type="italic">a Moabite should not enter into the congregation of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.23.3">Deut. xxiii. 3</reference>. These, it is likely, had approved themselves so hearty for the interest of Israel that in their case it was thought fit to dispense with that law, and the rather because it was an indication that the Son of David would have worthies among the Gentiles: with him there is neither Greek nor Jew.  <chapter eID="1Chr.11"/> <div eID="gen7747" type="x-p"/>

entries.8e8a7a26380ee5d826a0365ceab20d87b619851d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3721"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 11</title> <div sID="gen5328" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.1-1Chr.11.3">1Ch 11:1-3</reference>. David Made King.<div eID="gen5328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5329" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3721"/><hi type="bold">1. Then all Israel gathered themselves to David unto Hebron--</hi>This event happened on the death of Ish-bosheth (see on <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.1">2Sa 5:1</reference>). The convention of the estates of the kingdom, the public and solemn homage of the representatives of the people, and the repeated anointing of the new king in their presence and by their direction, seem to have been necessary to the general acknowledgment of the sovereign on the part of the nation (compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.11.15">1Sa 11:15</reference>).<div eID="gen5329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5330" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.4-1Chr.11.9">1Ch 11:4-9</reference>. He Wins the Castle of Zion from the Jebusites by Joab's Valor. <div eID="gen5330" type="x-p"/>
entries.9748f8c184cd1de34aef1f271cb2b83f653cd7c5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3722"/><div sID="gen5331" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3722"/><hi type="bold">4. David and all Israel went to ... Jebus--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.6">2Sa 5:6</reference>). <div eID="gen5331" type="x-p"/>
entries.4efc7ae69289a425e594f45fea084c733e08e91a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3723"/><div sID="gen5332" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3723"/><hi type="bold">8. Joab repaired the rest of the city--</hi>David built a new town to the north of the old one on Mount Zion; but Joab was charged with a commission to restore the part that had been occupied by the ancient Jebus, to repair the breaches made during the siege, to rebuild the houses which had been demolished or burned in the sacking of the town, and to preserve all that had escaped the violence of the soldiery. This work of reconstruction is not noticed elsewhere [Calmet].<div eID="gen5332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5333" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.10-1Chr.11.47">1Ch 11:10-47</reference>. A Catalogue of His Worthies. <div eID="gen5333" type="x-p"/>
entries.93e95ad275270b1b7c8923422cae3dc384dfa7d1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3724"/><div sID="gen5334" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3724"/><hi type="bold">10. These ... are the chief of the mighty men--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.8">2Sa 23:8</reference>). They are here described as those who held strongly with him (Margin) to make him king, &c. In these words the sacred historian assigns a reason for introducing the list of their names, immediately after his account of the election of David as king, and the conquest of Jerusalem; namely, that they assisted in making David king. In the original form of the list, and the connection in which it occurs in Samuel, there is no reference to the choice of a king; and even in this passage it is only in the clause introduced into the superscription that such a reference occurs [Keil]. <div eID="gen5334" type="x-p"/>
entries.85e3c252b3d0c94fe79e5b41f183b223e6fe8f20: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3725"/><div sID="gen5335" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3725"/><hi type="bold">11-13. Jashobeam, an Hachmonite--</hi>or, "son of Hachmoni." He is called also son of Zabdiel (<reference osisRef="1Chr.27.2">1Ch 27:2</reference>), so that, strictly speaking, he was the grandson of Hachmoni (compare <reference osisRef="1Chr.27.32">1Ch 27:32</reference>).<div eID="gen5335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5336" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lifted up his spear against three hundred slain by him at one time--</hi>The feat is said (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.8">2Sa 23:8</reference>) to have been a slaughter of eight hundred in one day. Some endeavor to reconcile the statements in that passage and in this by supposing that he slew eight hundred on one occasion and three hundred on another; while others conjecture that he attacked a body of eight hundred, and, having slain three hundred of them, the rest fled [Lightfoot]. <div eID="gen5336" type="x-p"/>
entries.901e1dffe84358f850b325f81e1d203376ddea60: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3728"/><div sID="gen5340" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3728"/><hi type="bold">15-19. David longed, and said, Oh that one would give me drink ... of the well of Beth-lehem--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.15">2Sa 23:15</reference>). This chivalrous act evinces the enthusiastic devotion of David's men, that they were ready to gratify his smallest wish at the risk of their lives. It is probable that, when uttering the wish, David had no recollection of the military posted at Beth-lehem. It is generally taken for granted that those who fought a way to the well of Beth-lehem were the three champions just mentioned [see on 1Ch 11:13]. But this is far from being clear. On the contrary, it would seem that three different heroes are referred to, for Abishai (<reference osisRef="1Chr.11.20">1Ch 11:20</reference>) was one of them. The camp of the Philistines was in the valley of Rephaim (<reference osisRef="1Chr.11.15">1Ch 11:15</reference>), which lay on the west of Jerusalem, but an outpost was stationed at Beth-lehem (<reference osisRef="1Chr.11.16">1Ch 11:16</reference>), and through this garrison they had to force a passage. <div eID="gen5340" type="x-p"/>
entries.d58c0cc8ad119d7d9e510168541e5a1677a54840: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3729"/><div sID="gen5341" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3729"/><hi type="bold">21. howbeit he attained not to the first three--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.19">2Sa 23:19</reference>). <div eID="gen5341" type="x-p"/>
entries.ad0e1d53d76a609712d3ce63bc3e5ce85a498380: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3730"/><div sID="gen5342" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3730"/><hi type="bold">22. Benaiah ... of Kabzeel--</hi>a town in the south of Judah (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.21">Jos 15:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.11.25">Ne 11:25</reference>). It is said that "he had done many acts," though three only are mentioned as specimens of his daring energy and fearless courage.<div eID="gen5342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5343" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">slew two lionlike men of Moab--</hi>literally, "lions of God," that is, great lions or champions. This gallant feat was probably achieved in David's hostile invasion of Moab (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.2">2Sa 8:2</reference>).<div eID="gen5343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5344" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">also he went down and slew a lion in a pit in a snowy day--</hi>probably a cave into which Benaiah had taken refuge from the snowstorm, and in which he encountered a savage lion which had its lair there. In a spacious cave the achievement would be far greater than if the monster had been previously snared or cabined in a pit. <div eID="gen5344" type="x-p"/>
entries.e6f19191d4095c1ad01b73ffa0916b78fba0e6ee: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3731"/><div sID="gen5345" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3731"/><hi type="bold">23. he went down--</hi>the ordinary phraseology for expressing an engagement in battle. The encounter of Benaiah with this gigantic Egyptian reminds us, in some respects, of David's combat with Goliath. At least, the height of this giant, which was about eight feet, and his armor, resembled his of Gath.<div eID="gen5345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5346" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with a staff--</hi>that is, having no other weapon in his hand than his walking stick. <div eID="gen5346" type="x-p"/>
entries.c93393838f44872b2cf2658d2ae47d47ff6b7a08: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3732"/><div sID="gen5347" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3732"/><hi type="bold">25. entries.c58f54053ad3aebbe7307455e44f818f837d9c9f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3733"/><div sID="gen5348" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3733"/><hi type="bold">26. entries.bc2b7a26972626683ef7e2292040be128a966da3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3734"/><div sID="gen5349" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3734"/><hi type="bold">27. Shammoth--</hi>Between this name and Hebez, that of Elikah has evidently fallen out, as we may see (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.25">2Sa 23:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.26">26</reference>) [Bertheau]. <div eID="gen5349" type="x-p"/>

Maharai--</hi>chief of the detachment of the guards who attended on the king in the tenth month, January (<reference osisRef="1Chr.27.13">1Ch 27:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.28">2Sa 23:28</reference>). <div eID="gen5350" type="x-p"/>
entries.a71af324a5ec6afb0c645e1b992b2c954a86cc52: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3736"/><div sID="gen5351" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3736"/><hi type="bold">39. Naharai--</hi>armorbearer to Joab (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.37">2Sa 23:37</reference>). The non-occurrence of Joab's name in any of the three catalogues is most probably to be accounted for by the circumstance that his office as commander-in-chief raised him to a position superior to all these orders of military knighthood. <div eID="gen5351" type="x-p"/>
entries.4fae5d153144f67f66b233fecefb9ceb5e20365d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3737"/><div sID="gen5352" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3737"/><hi type="bold">41. Uriah the Hittite--</hi>The enrolment of this name in such a list, attesting, as it does, his distinguished merits as a brave and devoted officer, aggravates the criminality of David's outrage on his life and honor. The number of the names at <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.26-1Chr.11.41">1Ch 11:26-41</reference> (exclusive of Asahel and Uriah, who were dead) is thirty, and at <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.41-1Chr.11.47">1Ch 11:41-47</reference> is sixteen--making together forty-eight (see on <reference osisRef="1Chr.27.1-1Chr.27.34">1Ch 27:1-34</reference>). Of those mentioned (<reference osisRef="1Chr.11.26-1Chr.11.41">1Ch 11:26-41</reference>), the greater part belonged to the tribes of Judah and Benjamin; the sixteen names (<reference osisRef="1Chr.11.41-1Chr.11.47">1Ch 11:41-47</reference>) are all associated with places unknown, or with cities and districts on the east of the Jordan. The northern tribes do not appear to have furnished any leaders [Bertheau]. <chapter eID="1Chr.11"/>

entries.85387cc8e965047d1aed32352b26013519dec022: <div eID="gen13573" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen13574" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13575" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13575" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13574" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13576" type="x-p"/> David is anointed king in Hebron, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.1-1Chr.11.3">1Chr 11:1-3</reference>. He wars against the Jebusites, and takes their city, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.4-1Chr.11.9">1Chr 11:4-9</reference>. An account of David's three mightiest heroes; and particularly of their hazardous exploit in bringing water from the well of Beth-lehem, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.10-1Chr.11.19">1Chr 11:10-19</reference>. A list of the rest, and an account of their acts, vv. 20-47. <div eID="gen13576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13577" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen13577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13578" type="x-p"/> Then all Israel gathered themselves to David - See <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.1-2Sam.5.10">2Sam 5:1-10</reference> (note), for the history contained in the first nine verses of this chapter, and the notes there.
entries.800ea3d5fa2625a413ea7da1ed04b2bcf0b4cfe6: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen13578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13579" type="x-p"/> The number of the mighty men - See <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.8">2Sam 23:8</reference> (note), etc., and the notes there. The Targum has a remarkable addition here. "These are the numbers of the strong men who were with David; he was the potent chief of the army; he sat upon the throne of judgment, anointed with the holy oil, all the prophets and wise men standing about him. When he went to battle, he was assisted from on high; and when he sat down to teach the law, the true meaning arose up in his mind. He was elect and pleasant, of a beautiful mien and lovely countenance, exercised in wisdom, prudent in counsel, and strong in virtue; the prince of the assembly, of a melodious voice, master in hymns, and chief among the mighty. He was instructed in the use of martial weapons; he carried a spear, to which was appended the ensign of the host of Judah; he went forth according to the voice of the Holy Spirit, was victorious in battle, and overthrew with his spear three hundred men at one time." - T. <div eID="gen13579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13580" type="x-p"/> On this and some of the following verses there is a judicious note of Dr. Kennicott, which I shall take the liberty to introduce, referring to his first Dissertation on the Hebrew text for farther illustration and proof, p. 128-144. "Among the parallel places, a comparison of which may be of very considerable service, scarce any passages will appear more effectually to correct each other than the catalogue of David's mighty men of valor, as it now stands in 2 Samuel 23:8-39, and in this chapter. About thirty-four Hebrew words have been lost out of this part of the passage in Chronicles, which are happily preserved in Samuel. "The chief point of proof is this, that the catalogue divides these thirty-seven warriors into the captain-general, a first three, a second three, and the remaining thirty; and yet that the third captain of the first ternary is now here omitted. The following juxtaposition will show the whole deficiency, and properly supply it. But let it be observed that Jashobeam, the first captain of the first ternary, had been already mentioned, and that the history is here speaking of the second captain, namely, Eleazar. 2 Samuel 1 Chronicles <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.9">2Sam 23:9</reference> And after him was Eleazar the son <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.12">1Chr 11:12</reference> And after him was Eleazar the son of Dodo, the Ahohite, one of the three mighty of Dodo, the Ahohite, who was one of the three mighties. men with David when they defied <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.13">1Chr 11:13</reference> He was with David at Pas-dammim, and there the Philistines that were there gathered together to the Philistines were gathered together to battle, and the men of Israel were gone away. battle, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.10">2Sam 23:10</reference> He arose and smote the Philistines until his hand was weary and his hand clave unto the sword; and the Lord wrought a great victory that day: and the people returned after him only to spoil. <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.11">2Sam 23:11</reference> And after him was Shammah. The son of Agee, the Hararite: and the Philistines were gathered together into a troop, where was where was a piece of ground full of lentiles: and the people a parcel of ground full of barley, and the people fled from the Philistines. <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.12">2Sam 23:12</reference> But he fled from before the Philistines. <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.14">1Chr 11:14</reference> And they set stood in the midst of the ground and defended themselves, in the midst of that parcel, and delivered it, and slew the Philistines: and the Lord it, and slew the Philistines: and the Lord wrought a great victory. saved them by a great deliverance.

entries.763771e5695927c32af51fb1615e35acb9e677c5: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen13581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13582" type="x-p"/> Benaiah - slew two lion-like men of Moab - The Targum says, "Benaiah was a valiant man, fearing sin, and of a righteous conduct in Kabzeel; he slew two of the nobles of Moab, who were like two strong lions. entries.7dac11159774f8280143078fc9214f3e0411da7a: <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.1-1Chr.11.3">1Ch 11:1-3</reference> <hi type="italic">The anointing of David to be king over the whole of Israel in Hebron;</hi> cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.1">2Sa 5:1</reference>-3. - After Saul’s death, in obedience to a divine intimation, David left Ziklag, whither he had withdrawn himself before the decisive battle between the Philistines and the Israelites, and betook himself with his wives and his warriors to Hebron, and was there anointed by the men of Judah to be king over their tribe (<reference osisRef="2Sam.2.1-2Sam.2.4">2Sa 2:1-4</reference>). But Abner, the captain of Saul’s host, led Ishbosheth, Saul’s son, with the remainder of the defeated army of the Israelites, to Mahanaim in Gilead, and there made him king over Gilead, and gradually also, as he reconquered it from the Philistines, over the land of Israel, over Jezreel, Ephraim, Benjamin, and all (the remainder of) Israel, with the exception of the tribal domain of Judah. Ishbosheth’s kingship did not last longer than two years, while David reigned over Judah in Hebron for seven years and a half (<reference osisRef="2Sam.2.10">2Sa 2:10</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Sam.2.11">2Sa 2:11</reference>). When Abner advanced with Ishbosheth’s army from Mahanaim against Gibeon, he was defeated by Joab, David’s captain, so that he was obliged again to withdraw beyond Jordan (2 Sam 2:12-32); and although the struggle between the house of Saul and the house of David still continued, yet the house of Saul waxed ever weaker, while David’s power increased. At length, when Ishbosheth reproached the powerful Abner because of a concubine of his father’s, he threatened that he would transfer the crown of Israel to David, and carried his threat into execution without delay. He imparted his design to the elders of Israel and Benjamin; and when they had given their consent, he made his way to Hebron, and announced to David the submission of all Israel to his sway (2 Sam 3:1-21). Abner, indeed, did not fully carry out the undertaking; for on his return journey he was assassinated by Joab, without David’s knowledge, and against his will. Immediately afterwards, Ishbosheth, who had become powerless and spiritless through terror at Abner’s death, was murdered in his own house by two of the leaders of his army. There now remained of Saul’s family only Jonathan’s son Mephibosheth (<reference osisRef="2Sam.4.1-2Sam.4.12">2Sa 4:1-12</reference>), then not more than twelve years old, and lame in both his feet, and all the tribes of Israel determined to anoint David to be their king. The carrying out of this resolution is narrated in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.1-1Chr.11.3">1Ch 11:1-3</reference>, in complete agreement as to the facts with <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.1-2Sam.5.3">2Sa 5:1-3</reference>, where the matter has been already commented upon. In ch. 12 23-40 there follows a more detailed account of the assembly of the tribes of Israel in Hebron. The last words in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.3">1Ch 11:3</reference>, וגו יהוה כּדבר, are a didactic addition of the author of the Chronicle, which has been derived from <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.13">1Sa 16:13</reference> and 1Sa 15:28. In <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.4-2Sam.5.5">2Sa 5:4-5</reference>, in accordance with the custom of the author of the books of Samuel and Kings to state the age and duration of the reign of each of the kings immediately after the announcement of their entry upon their office, there follows after the preceding a statement of the duration of David’s reign; cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.1">1Sa 13:1</reference>; 2Sa 2:10., 1Ki 14:21; 1Ki 15:2, etc. This remark is to be found in the Chronicle only at the close of David’s reign; see <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.29">1Ch 29:29</reference>, which shows that Thenius’ opinion that this verse has been omitted from the Chronicle by a mistake is not tenable.
entries.f075cfea6f731a85488bc0e24119d79dee02b453: <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.4-1Chr.11.9">1Ch 11:4-9</reference> <hi type="italic">The capture of the citadel of Zion, and Jerusalem chosen to be the royal residence under the name of the city of David;</hi> cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.6-2Sam.5.10">2Sa 5:6-10</reference>, and the commentary on this section at that place. - יחיּה, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.8">1Ch 11:8</reference>, to make alive, is used here, as in <reference osisRef="Neh.4.2">Neh 4:2</reference>, of the rebuilding of ruins. The general remark, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.9">1Ch 11:9</reference>, “and David increased continually in might,” etc., opens the way for the transition to the history of David’s reign which follows. As a proof of his increasing greatness, there follows in
entries.a08be01f579378857c9a1c9cf5ea5bede3a66754: <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.10-1Chr.11.14">1Ch 11:10-14</reference> <hi type="italic">A register of the heroes</hi> who stood by him in the establishment of his kingdom. The greater part of this register is found in 2 Sam 23:8-39 also, though there are many divergences in the names, which for the most part have found their way into one or other of the texts by errors of transcription. The conclusion (<reference osisRef="1Chr.11.41-1Chr.11.47">1Ch 11:41-47</reference> of the Chronicle) is not found in 2 Sam 23, either because the author of the Chronicle followed another and older register than that used by the author of the book of Samuel, or because the latter has not communicated all the names contained in his authority. The former of these is the more probable supposition. In the Chronicle the superscription of the register is enlarged by the insertion in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.10">1Ch 11:10</reference>, before the simple superscription in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="1Chr.11.11">1Ch 11:11</reference></hi>, cf. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="2Sam.23.8">2Sa 23:8</reference></hi>, of a further superscription informing us of the design which the chronicler had in introducing the register at this place. “These are the chiefs of David’s heroes who stood by him strongly (עם התחזּק, as <reference osisRef="Dan.10.21">Dan 10:21</reference>) in his kingdom, with the whole of Israel to make him king, according to the word of Jahve, over Israel.” The collocation הגּבּרים ראשׁי is accounted for by the fact that הגּבּור is a designation of a valiant or heroic man in general, without reference to his position, whether co-ordinate with or subordinate to others. Among David’s גּבּרים who helped to establish his kingdom, are not merely those who are mentioned by name in the following register, but also, as we learn from 1 Chron 12, the great number of valiant men of all the tribes, who, even during his persecution by Saul, crowded round him, and immediately after Saul’s death came to him in Hebron to hail him king. The enumeration in our passage contains only the chiefs, ראשׁים, of those valiant men, i.e., those who held the first rank among them, and who were in great part leaders in the army of David, or became so. להמליכו is not to be confined to the mere appointment to the kingship, but includes also his establishment in it; for there follows an account of the heroic deeds which the men enumerated by name performed in the wars which David waged against his enemies in order to maintain and increase his kingly power. יהוה דּבר יהוה .rewop concerning Israel is the word of the Lord, the import of which is recorded in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.3">1Ch 11:3</reference>, that David should feed His people Israel, and be ruler over them. The <hi type="italic">ipsissima verba</hi> are not found in the earlier history of David, but the substance of them has been deduced from <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.13">1Sa 16:13</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.28">1Sa 15:28</reference>; cf. herewith the remarks on 2Sa 3:18. The enumeration of these heroes is introduced in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.11">1Ch 11:11</reference> by a short supplementary superscription, “these the number of the heroes.” That מספּר should be used instead of the שׁמות of Samuel is surprising, but is explained by the fact that these heroes at first constituted a corps whose designation was derived from their number. They originally amounted to thirty, whence they are still called the thirty, השּׁלשׁים; cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.12">1Ch 11:12</reference>, and the discussion on 2Sa 23:8. In both narratives three classes are distinguished. <div eID="gen5689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5690" type="x-p"/> Jashobeam, Eleazar, and Shammah hold the first place, and specially bold and heroic deeds performed by them are recorded, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.11-1Chr.11.14">1Ch 11:11-14</reference>, and <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.8">2Sa 23:8</reference>-12. For details as to themselves and their deeds, see on the last cited passage. There we have already remarked, that in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.13">1Ch 11:13</reference> of the text of the Chronicle, the three lines which in Samuel come between שׁם נאספוּ בּפּלשׁתּים (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.9">2Sa 23:9</reference>) and פלשׁתּים ויּעספוּ, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.11">1Ch 11:11</reference>, have been, through wandering of the copyist’s eye, omitted; and with them the name of the third hero, שׁמּה, has also been dropped, so that the heroic deed done by him, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="1Chr.11.13">1Ch 11:13</reference></hi>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.14">1Ch 11:14</reference>, appears, according to our present text, to have been performed by Eleazar. In place of the words, “And the Philistines had gathered themselves together there to battle, and there was a parcel of ground full of barley,” <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.13">1Ch 11:13</reference>, the text, according to the narrative in <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.11">2Sa 23:11</reference>, must have stood originally thus: “The Philistines had gathered themselves together there to battle, and the men of Israel went up (sc., retreating from the Philistines up the mountain); he, however, stood firm, and smote the Philistines till his hand was wearied, and cleaved unto the sword (i.e., clung crampedly to his sword through fatigue): there wrought Jahve a great deliverance on that day, and the people returned (from their flight) behind him only to spoil. And after him was Shammah the son of Aga the Hararite, and the Philistines had gathered themselves together to battle,” etc. In <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.14">1Ch 11:14</reference> the plural forms יתיצּבוּ, ויּצּילוּה, ויּכּוּ, are incorrect, and should be changed into singulars, as in <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.12">2Sa 23:12</reference>, since only the deed of the hero Shammah is here spoken of. The plurals were probably introduced into the text after the missing lines had been dropped out by a reader or copyist, who, on account of the דּייד עם היה הוּא (<reference osisRef="1Chr.11.13">1Ch 11:13</reference>), understood the three clauses of <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.14">1Ch 11:14</reference> to refer to Eleazar and David. ויּושׁע, on the contrary, is here perfectly appropriate, and is not to be altered to suit the ויּעשׂ of Samuel, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.14">1Ch 11:14</reference>, for the καὶ ἐποίησε of the lxx is not of itself a sufficient reason for doing so.
entries.59b6d09c20af399a07b85e13345e1973376a9107: <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.15-1Chr.11.19">1Ch 11:15-19</reference> <div eID="gen5690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5691" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.15-1Chr.11.19">1Ch 11:15-19</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.13-2Sam.23.17">2Sa 23:13-17</reference>) there follows an exploit of three others of the thirty, whose names have not been handed down. ראשׁ השּׁלושׁים, the thirty chiefs (not, as Thenius wrongly interprets the words, these three knights the chief parts, i.e., these three chief knights), are David’s heroes hereafter mentioned, the thirty-two heroes of the third class named in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.26-1Chr.11.40">1Ch 11:26-40</reference> (or vv. 24-39 of Samuel). That three others, different from the before-mentioned Jashobeam, Eleazar, and Shammah are intended, is plain from the omission of the article with שׁלושׁה; for if these three were spoken of, we would have השׁלושׁה, as in 1Ch 11:18. For further remarks on this exploit, which was probably performed in the war treated of in 1Ch 14:8., and in 2Sa 5:17., see on <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.13">2Sa 23:13</reference>-17. The words וגו האנשׁים הדם, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.19">1Ch 11:19</reference>, are to be translated, “The blood of these men shall I drink in their souls? for for their souls (i.e., for the price of their souls, at the risk of their life) have they brought it.” The expression “blood in their souls” is to be understood according to <reference osisRef="Gen.9.4">Gen 9:4</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lev.17.14">Lev 17:14</reference> (הוּא בנפשׁו דּמו, “his blood is in the soul,” is that which constitutes his soul). As there blood and soul are used synonymously (the blood as seat of and container of the soul, and the soul as floating in the blood), so here David, according to our account of his words, compares the water, which those heroes had brought for the price of their souls, to the souls of the men, and the drinking of the water to the drinking of their souls, and finally the souls to the blood, in order to express his abhorrence of such a draught. The meaning therefore may be thus expressed: “Shall I drink in this water the souls, and so the blood, of these men; for they have brought the water even for the price of their souls?”
entries.51663a9a21e808ed31117999382d8e80931700d0: <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.20-1Chr.11.25">1Ch 11:20-25</reference> <div eID="gen5691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5692" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.20-1Chr.11.25">1Ch 11:20-25</reference> the second class of heroes, to which Abshai (Abishai) and Benaiah belonged, cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.18-2Sam.23.23">2Sa 23:18-23</reference>, is spoken of. They were not equal to the preceding three in heroic deeds, but yet stood higher than the list of heroes which follows in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.26">1Ch 11:26</reference> and onwards. אבשׁי, as <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.16">1Ch 2:16</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.10">2Sa 10:10</reference>, while in <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.18">2Sa 23:18</reference> and elsewhere he is called אבישׁי, was one of the three sons of Zeruiah (<reference osisRef="1Chr.2.16">1Ch 2:16</reference>). It is difficult to explain השׁלושׁה ראשׁ, “he was the chief of the three,” instead of which we find in <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.23">2Sa 23:23</reference> השׁלשׁי, i.e., השּׁלשׁי, “chief of the body-guard” (knights). But owing to the succeeding שׁם (ולו) בּשּׁלושׁה ולא, where Samuel also has בּשּׁלשׁה, and to the recurrence of השׁלושׁה on two occasions in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.21">1Ch 11:21</reference> (cf. 2 <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.19">2Sa 23:19</reference>), it does not seem possible to alter the text with Thenius. Bertheau proposes to get rid of the difficulty by taking the word שׁלושׁה in two different significations-on the one hand as denoting the numeral three, and on the other as being an abstract substantive, “the totality of the thirty.” He justifies the latter signification by comparison of <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.21">1Ch 11:21</reference> with <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.25">1Ch 11:25</reference>, and of <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.19">2Sa 23:19</reference> with <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.23">1Ch 11:23</reference>, from which he deduces that שׁלושׁה and שׁלושׁים denote a larger company, in which both Abishai and Benaiah held a prominent place. But this signification cannot be made good from these passages. In both clauses of <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.25">1Ch 11:25</reference> (and <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.23">2Sa 23:23</reference>) השּׁלשׁים and השּׁלשׁה are contrasted, which would rather go to prove the contrary of Bertheau’s proposition, viz., that השּׁלשׁה, the three, cannot at the same time denote the whole of the thirty, השּׁלשׁים. The truth of the matter may be gathered from a comparison of <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.18">1Ch 11:18</reference> with 1Ch 11:15. In <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.18">1Ch 11:18</reference> השּׁלשׁה is synonymous with השּׁלושׁים מן השׁלושׁה, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.15">1Ch 11:15</reference>; i.e., the three in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.18">1Ch 11:18</reference> are the same men who in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.15">1Ch 11:15</reference>, where they are first met with, are called three of the thirty; and consequently השּׁלשׁה, the three (triad), <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.21">1Ch 11:21</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.25">1Ch 11:25</reference>, can only denote the triad of heroes previously named. This is placed beyond doubt by a comparison of <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.24">1Ch 11:24</reference> with <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.25">1Ch 11:25</reference>, since the הגּבּרים שׁלושׁה, the triad of heroes, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.24">1Ch 11:24</reference>, corresponds to the simple השּׁלשׁה of 1Ch 11:25. The only remaining question is, whether by this triad of heroes we are to understand those spoken of in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.11-1Chr.11.14">1Ch 11:11-14</reference>, - Jashobeam, Eleazar, and Shammah, - or the three whose names are not given, but whose exploit is narrated in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.15">1Ch 11:15</reference>-19. But the circumstance that the names of the three latter are not mentioned goes decidedly to show that השּׁלשׁה in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.20-1Chr.11.25">1Ch 11:20-25</reference> does not denote that nameless triad, whose exploit is manifestly adduced incidentally only as a similar case, but the three most valiant, who held the first rank among David’s heroes. Bertheau’s opinion, that in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.20-1Chr.11.25">1Ch 11:20-25</reference> one triad of heroes is distinguished from another, cannot be regarded as well-founded, for the three of whom Abishai was chief are not distinguished, and are not different from the three to whom, according to <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.21">1Ch 11:21</reference>, he did not attain. Nor is there greater reason to believe that the triad of <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.20">1Ch 11:20</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.21">1Ch 11:21</reference> is different from that in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.24">1Ch 11:24</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.25">1Ch 11:25</reference>, among whom Benaiah made himself a name, and to whom he did not attain. The fact of being chief or prince over the three is not irreconcilably contradictory to the statement that he did not attain to them, i.e., did not come up to them in heroic strength, as is shown by the two classes being connected in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="1Chr.11.21">1Ch 11:21</reference></hi>. As to the rank which the triad held in the regular forces of David, we know nothing further than that Jashobeam was, according to <reference osisRef="1Chr.27.2">1Ch 27:2</reference>, leader of that part of the army which was on duty during the first month. Eleazar the son of Dodo, and the Hararite Shammah the son of Aga, are not mentioned anywhere but in our list. Abishai, on the contrary, who had already distinguished himself by his audacious courage in David’s struggle with Saul (1Sa 26:6.), conducted together with Joab the war against Abner (2 Sam 2:24-3:30). Afterwards, in David’s war with the Ammonites, he was under Joab in command of the second half of the host (2Sa 10:10.); in the war against Absalom he commanded a third part of the host (1Ch 18:2.); and in the struggle with the rebel Sheba he commanded the vanguard of the royal troops sent against the rebel (1Ch 20:6.); and in general held, along with Joab the commander-in-chief, the first place among David’s captains. In this position he was chief of the three heroes before mentioned, and their leader (שׂר), and among them had made himself a name. ולא, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.20">1Ch 11:20</reference>, is an orthographical error for ולו, as in fifteen other passages, according to the Masora. See on <reference osisRef="Exod.21.10">Exo 21:10</reference> and Isa 63:9.

entries.4e87351c50c5ec333651a9b2c2e6d7d0dccd79d8: <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.47">1Ch 11:47</reference> המּצביה, which, so far as the form is concerned, is not a nomen gentil., Reland (<hi type="italic">Palaest. ill.</hi> p. 899) holds for a contraction of צבעויא מגדל, Migdal Zebujah-a place which, according to the rabbins, is said to have been somewhere in the neighbourhood of Hebron. Bertheau’s opinion is, that the article has come into the text by mistake; and when it has been struck out, the remaining consonants, מצביה, recall the מצּבה of <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.36">2Sa 23:36</reference> (?). Registers of the Valiant Men Who Helped David to the Kingdom - 1 Chronicles 12 <div eID="gen5694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5695" type="x-p"/> This chapter contains two somewhat long registers, viz.: (1) a register of the valiant men who before Saul’s death went over to David, vv. 1-22; and (2) a register of the fighting men who anointed him king in Hebron. The first is divided into three smaller registers: (<hi type="italic">a</hi>) that of the valiant Benjamites who came to David during his stay in Ziklag (<reference osisRef="1Chr.12.1-1Chr.12.7">1Ch 12:1-7</reference>); (<hi type="italic">b</hi>) that of the Gadites and the men of Judah and Benjamin who went over to him while he remained in the mountain fastnesses; and (<hi type="italic">c</hi>) that of the Manassites who, on his return to Ziklag before Saul’s last battle with the Philistines, joined themselves to him (<reference osisRef="1Chr.12.19-1Chr.12.22">1Ch 12:19-22</reference>).  <chapter eID="1Chr.11"/> <div eID="gen5695" type="x-p"/>
